records.name: Mediterranean Sea
records.subtitle: A semi-enclosed sea linking three continents

sections.title: Between three continents
sections.body: The Mediterranean lies between Europe, North Africa and western Asia, linked to the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar. Its coasts contain islands, deltas, deep basins and relatively narrow passages. The sea has influenced where settlements developed and how people transported goods for thousands of years. It is not one uniform environment: conditions around the Adriatic, Aegean and western basin can differ markedly.

sections.title: Water exchange and ecosystems
sections.body: Evaporation, river input and exchange with Atlantic water influence the sea's salinity and circulation. Seagrass meadows and rocky habitats support important marine life, while coral-like communities and deep environments provide additional ecological variety. The region contains species found nowhere else and many species introduced through shipping or waterways. These relationships are sensitive to temperature changes and pressures along densely inhabited coasts.

sections.title: A long maritime history
sections.body: Greek, Roman, North African, Levantine and many other societies developed connections across Mediterranean routes. Travellers carried agricultural products, languages, technologies and ideas, while warfare and forced movement also shaped the region. The sea's history belongs to no single civilisation. Harbours and coastal ruins reveal particular periods, but fishing communities and ordinary seafarers were equally part of maritime life.

sections.title: Conservation across borders
sections.body: Fishing pressure, wastewater, tourism and climate warming affect different sections of the Mediterranean. Regional coordination under the Barcelona Convention provides one framework for responding to shared concerns. The sea illustrates why protecting a coastal reserve is useful but cannot alone solve problems generated beyond its boundaries. Understanding the Mediterranean involves tracing water movement and human networks together.

records.quickFact: The Mediterranean lies between Europe, North Africa and western Asia, linked to the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar.

records.name: Baltic Sea
records.subtitle: Brackish water and a complex coastal catchment

sections.title: A sea with unusually fresh water
sections.body: The Baltic Sea lies between northern and eastern European countries and connects to the North Sea through relatively narrow Danish waters. River inflows and restricted exchange make much of it brackish, with salinity varying between sub-basins. Its shallow shelves, archipelagos and deeper areas create different habitats. The coastal geography helps explain why water quality problems can persist for long periods.

sections.title: Nutrients and oxygen
sections.body: Nitrogen and phosphorus enter the sea from a large catchment that includes farms, settlements and rivers. Excess nutrients can stimulate algal growth and reduce oxygen in deeper waters as organic matter decomposes. HELCOM identifies eutrophication as a major ecological pressure. The effect is not identical everywhere: mixing, temperature and the shape of each basin influence how water and oxygen circulate.

sections.title: Ports and shared histories
sections.body: The Baltic linked trading towns and coastal peoples through maritime routes, including those of the Hanseatic network. Fishing, shipbuilding and modern freight remain connected to its shores. Different languages and political histories meet around the basin, but the physical water system crosses those borders. Decisions about nutrients, shipping or fisheries in one part of the catchment can affect other countries.

sections.title: A changing coastal environment
sections.body: Winter ice conditions vary with latitude and weather, while warming and changing runoff can affect marine organisms. Long-term monitoring is necessary to distinguish seasonal variation from environmental trends. Protecting the Baltic means considering inland land use as well as the sea itself. It is a useful case study of how a nearly enclosed basin reflects the combined effects of rivers, cities and climate.

records.quickFact: The Baltic Sea lies between northern and eastern European countries and connects to the North Sea through relatively narrow Danish waters.

records.name: North Sea
records.subtitle: A working continental-shelf sea

sections.title: Water over a broad shelf
sections.body: The North Sea lies between Britain, Scandinavia and north-western mainland Europe. Much of it occupies a relatively shallow continental shelf, although depths vary considerably and the Norwegian Trench forms a deeper feature. Atlantic exchange and strong tides help shape its circulation. Sandy seabeds, estuaries, gravel areas and coastal wetlands create a varied marine landscape closely connected to densely populated shorelines.

sections.title: Fish and marine wildlife
sections.body: Plankton production sustains food webs that include commercial fish, seabirds and marine mammals. Conditions differ with season and location, and not all seabed habitats respond alike to disturbance. Fishing and changes to water temperature can alter ecosystems. The sea therefore requires scientific monitoring rather than a single estimate of how much marine life it contains.

sections.title: Shipping and offshore energy
sections.body: Major European ports depend on North Sea routes, while offshore oil, gas and wind installations use its shelf and weather conditions. Pipelines, cables and sand extraction create further demands on space. These activities support economies but can conflict with conservation or other uses of the sea. Maritime planning has to consider navigational safety, habitats and the interests of several neighbouring countries.

sections.title: Coasts in motion
sections.body: Tides, storms and sediment movement reshape coastal dunes, mudflats and estuaries. Sea-level change creates continuing questions about flood protection and habitat management. Understanding the North Sea requires linking offshore conditions with the rivers and settlements around it. Its importance lies in being both a productive ecosystem and one of the world's most intensively used marine regions.

records.quickFact: The North Sea lies between Britain, Scandinavia and north-western mainland Europe.

records.name: Black Sea
records.subtitle: A basin with unusual deep-water chemistry

sections.title: A sea with a narrow connection
sections.body: The Black Sea lies between south-eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Anatolia, connected to the Mediterranean system through the Turkish straits. Major rivers flow into it, supplying freshwater and sediment from a very large catchment. The contrast between river inflow and saline water entering through the straits affects its layered circulation. Its surface habitats differ greatly from conditions far below.

sections.title: Why deep water matters
sections.body: Much of the Black Sea's deeper water has very little available oxygen, with chemical conditions unlike those in its upper layers. Density differences and limited vertical mixing are important parts of the explanation. Marine life in the surface and shelf zones still supports fisheries and ecosystems. It would be wrong to describe the entire sea as lifeless because its deep basin is anoxic.

sections.title: Ports, rivers and histories
sections.body: The Black Sea has been a route for trade and migration among communities along its coasts. River corridors connect its shores with distant inland regions, while changing political borders shaped its port cities. Shipping, fishing and coastal tourism are important in different areas. The cultural history belongs to many peoples, not one modern country.

sections.title: Pressures beyond the coastline
sections.body: Pollution and nutrient input from rivers can affect coastal water quality, while warming, fishing and other activities create additional ecological pressure. Monitoring oxygen and water exchange is important for understanding change. The Black Sea illustrates how the shape of a basin and its links with surrounding land can create unusual chemical conditions and complex conservation challenges.

records.quickFact: The Black Sea lies between south-eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Anatolia, connected to the Mediterranean system through the Turkish straits.

records.name: Red Sea
records.subtitle: Coral reefs alongside an arid coastline

sections.title: A narrow sea between continents
sections.body: The Red Sea lies between north-eastern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, connecting northwards with the Suez region and southwards through Bab el-Mandeb towards the Gulf of Aden. Its long, narrow form reflects tectonic processes that have pulled landmasses apart. Shelves and deep troughs create different habitats. Extensive dry coastlines make the contrast between desert land and productive marine ecosystems especially striking.

sections.title: Reefs in warm, salty water
sections.body: The Red Sea supports coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove habitats despite warm conditions and relatively high salinity. Protected areas off Sudan illustrate the diversity of reef structures and the wildlife they sustain, including fish, turtles and marine mammals. The habitats are connected through currents and animal movement, so conserving a single reef requires attention to wider marine conditions.

sections.title: Routes and coastal communities
sections.body: Maritime routes across the Red Sea have linked African and Arabian communities over long periods. The Suez Canal greatly changed global shipping patterns by connecting the Mediterranean and Red Sea systems. Fishing and coastal livelihoods also depend on the water. Political borders divide the coastline, but currents, reefs and migratory species cross them.

sections.title: A sensitive region
sections.body: Corals face risks from warming, pollution and damaging marine activity, even where individual reefs show unusual tolerance to high temperatures. Research into these ecosystems must avoid assuming they are immune to change. Studying the Red Sea offers a way to connect plate tectonics, international transport, desert geography and the delicate biology of reef habitats.

records.quickFact: The Red Sea lies between north-eastern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, connecting northwards with the Suez region and southwards through Bab el-Mandeb towards the Gulf of Aden.

records.name: Caribbean Sea
records.subtitle: Islands, reefs and currents

sections.title: A sea bordered by islands and mainland
sections.body: The Caribbean Sea lies south of many Caribbean islands and north of South America's coast, connected with the Atlantic through several passages. Its waters include deep basins, continental margins and complex island shelves. Different coastlines support mangroves, reefs and sandy beaches. The region is not environmentally uniform: a deep offshore basin and a sheltered coastal lagoon can function very differently.

sections.title: Marine ecosystems linked together
sections.body: Coral reefs provide habitat for numerous species, while seagrass beds and mangroves can support nurseries and protect parts of the coastline. Currents connect some populations across national boundaries. Warming, pollution and changes in fishing can affect these relationships. Healthy reefs depend on water quality and wider ecological processes, not just the visible coral structures.

sections.title: History on maritime routes
sections.body: Indigenous Caribbean societies existed long before European colonisation, and their histories should not be erased by accounts focused on later voyages. Colonisation, plantation economies, forced labour, migration and exchange transformed coastal communities. The sea connected islands and mainland ports through trade, fishing and travel. Its cultural geography remains diverse in languages, institutions and traditions.

sections.title: Working together on protection
sections.body: Many countries and territories share responsibility for a connected marine environment. UNEP's Caribbean Environment Programme supports regional cooperation on biodiversity and pollution. Hurricane exposure, coastal development and changing sea conditions can also affect communities. The Caribbean is a useful example of why protecting marine ecosystems and understanding human history need to be approached together.

records.quickFact: The Caribbean Sea lies south of many Caribbean islands and north of South America's coast, connected with the Atlantic through several passages.

records.name: Bering Sea
records.subtitle: A productive subarctic shelf

sections.title: A sea between Alaska and Asia
sections.body: The Bering Sea lies between Alaska and north-eastern Asia, extending towards the Bering Strait and the Pacific. Its broad continental shelf and deeper western basin create very different ocean environments. Seasonal sea ice affects much of the northern area, although its position changes between years. The contrast between shallow shelf and open water helps explain why the region supports productive marine food webs.

sections.title: Life shaped by ice and nutrients
sections.body: Plankton blooms depend on light, nutrients and seasonal conditions. Fish, seabirds, seals and other mammals are connected through feeding relationships that can shift as ice and temperature conditions change. NOAA researchers study how such changes affect groundfish populations and wider ecosystems. A single good fishing season cannot establish the health of the marine environment over decades.

sections.title: Communities and fisheries
sections.body: Commercial fisheries are economically important, while Indigenous communities have long relationships with marine resources and coastal ecosystems. Decisions about harvesting, conservation and climate adaptation need to acknowledge different kinds of knowledge and rights. The Bering Sea is also a place of international scientific and management concerns rather than a simple boundary between continents.

sections.title: Monitoring change
sections.body: Scientists use surveys and environmental observations to investigate plankton, water conditions and animal populations. Shifts in sea ice can influence food availability in ways that vary across species. The Bering Sea provides an important example of how a relatively remote marine region can matter greatly to coastal communities and to the broader Pacific ecosystem.

records.quickFact: The Bering Sea lies between Alaska and north-eastern Asia, extending towards the Bering Strait and the Pacific.

records.name: Sea of Okhotsk
records.subtitle: Seasonal ice along the north-west Pacific

sections.title: A sea bordered by Russia and Japan
sections.body: The Sea of Okhotsk lies north of Japan, bounded in part by the Russian mainland, Sakhalin and the Kuril island chain. Its southern openings link it with other Pacific waters, while its northern areas experience severe winters. Shelf waters, islands and deeper basins create varied habitats. The sea's seasonal ice is one of its most recognisable physical features.

sections.title: Ice that changes through the year
sections.body: Cold air and regional currents help produce extensive winter sea ice, much of which retreats during warmer months. The Japan Meteorological Agency tracks its maximum area and reports a long-term decline amid large year-to-year variations. Monitoring is important because ice affects light, water mixing and marine food chains. One unusually icy or ice-free season should not be confused with the longer trend.

sections.title: Productive waters and coastal lives
sections.body: Marine ecosystems support fish, seabirds and mammals, with resources used by coastal communities and commercial fleets. Currents and seasonal conditions influence where organisms feed. The sea's borders involve different jurisdictions, adding complexity to scientific cooperation and resource management. Fishing pressure and climatic changes can interact in ways that require careful observation.

sections.title: More than a frozen surface
sections.body: The Okhotsk region includes coastal wetlands, volcanic islands and deep marine habitats as well as floating ice. Its distinctive character comes from the interaction of geography and climate. Understanding it helps explain how changes in cold-region ocean processes can affect wildlife, transport and neighbouring communities even in places far from polar ice sheets.

records.quickFact: The Sea of Okhotsk lies north of Japan, bounded in part by the Russian mainland, Sakhalin and the Kuril island chain.

records.name: Weddell Sea
records.subtitle: Antarctic sea ice and deep water formation

sections.title: Along the Antarctic coast
sections.body: The Weddell Sea lies on the Atlantic-facing side of Antarctica, where sea ice, floating ice shelves and open water change with seasons. Strong winds, extreme cold and the surrounding continental shelf influence conditions. Much of the region is difficult to observe directly, which makes measurements by satellites, research vessels and autonomous instruments especially valuable.

sections.title: Ice and the ocean beneath
sections.body: Sea ice forms at the surface, while large ice shelves extend from land-based glaciers into the sea. These are different kinds of ice and affect water in different ways. Cooling and changes in salinity can contribute to formation of dense water in parts of the Southern Ocean. Understanding those processes matters because ocean circulation connects the Antarctic region with distant basins.

sections.title: Food webs in cold water
sections.body: Phytoplankton provide the basis for food webs involving krill, fish, seabirds, seals and whales. Light and ice conditions influence when marine productivity is greatest. Animals may depend on different habitats through their life cycles, and changes in sea ice can create varied outcomes for different species. The ecosystem cannot be described as uniformly barren because temperatures are low.

sections.title: Science across changing seasons
sections.body: Researchers investigate ice history, chemistry and circulation to understand how the Weddell Sea responds to environmental change. Records can be difficult to interpret because seasonal timing matters as well as overall ice extent. The region illustrates the importance of long-term observations in polar science and the way local Antarctic processes can have wider climatic implications.

records.quickFact: The Weddell Sea lies on the Atlantic-facing side of Antarctica, where sea ice, floating ice shelves and open water change with seasons.
